narrate.summary: This paper develops standard errors for causal effect estimates when treatment assignments have known but potentially complicated dependence across units. It represents potential outcomes as items in a finite population and estimates their mean with inverse-probability weighting. The method builds a graph linking pairs of outcomes that cannot be observed together, then uses the graph’s connected components to adjust the variance estimate. The resulting connected-components (CC) estimator is an unbiased estimate of an upper bound on the design-based variance, with the gap depending on treatment-effect heterogeneity across components. The authors find that it performs well in theory, simulations, and two applications, often yielding shorter standard errors than competing methods.
narrate.key_results: The estimator reduces to the Neyman variance estimator in completely randomized experiments and to a cluster-robust variance estimator in cluster-randomized experiments; the authors also prove it is admissible among quadratic-form variance estimators. In simulations based on the Paluck school-network study, nominal 95% confidence intervals from the CC estimator had coverage of at least 93.5%, and their average widths were 44% to 84% of the Aronow–Samii widths across the direct-effect specifications. In the Paluck data, the CC standard error was shortest in 7 of 8 specifications, and in the most extreme case was less than half the alternatives; the estimator was computed in under 1 second, while some comparison optimizations took up to 31 hours. In simulations and the application based on Pollmann’s spatial-treatment data, CC confidence intervals were about three times shorter than Pollmann’s, with near-nominal coverage in the simulations using true scores.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the main estimator requires more than one connected component and relies on a correctly specified exposure mapping. It can be conservative when treatment-effect sums vary across components, and the general framework does not itself establish the central limit theorems needed to justify normal-based confidence intervals in every setting.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The graph and joint observation probabilities may be difficult to construct in large or intricate designs; the paper’s applications estimate assignment probabilities using five million simulated assignments, but do not establish computational scaling for broader settings. Empirical evaluation is limited to two application settings, and the spatial application uses a public dataset simulated to resemble proprietary data rather than the original data.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying whether outcome-distribution information or covariates can reduce conservativeness, extending the method to continuous treatment exposures, developing more general central limit theorems, and analyzing performance when exposure mappings are misspecified.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A practical next step would be to provide software and scalable procedures for calculating joint observation probabilities and constructing the graph, including diagnostics for probabilities estimated by simulation. The method could also be evaluated prospectively in additional designed experiments and under operational constraints such as sequential assignment or restrictions on feasible treatment allocations.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for Bayesian experimental design that estimates the information available from an experiment using the entropy of the evidence distribution. It applies when the likelihood entropy is independent of the design or can be calculated explicitly, including additive Gaussian noise models. The method maps prior samples or numerical integration points through an approximate forward model and uses them to construct a Gaussian mixture approximation to the evidence. It then estimates the mixture’s entropy, avoiding the nested integrations used in direct expected information gain estimation. The authors prove convergence results and report numerical experiments showing faster convergence with quasi-Monte Carlo points than with ordinary Monte Carlo samples.
narrate.key_results: For Monte Carlo construction, the authors establish a root-mean-squared error rate of order δ_K plus M to the power negative one-half plus N to the power negative one-half. For first-order quasi-Monte Carlo construction, the rate in M is nearly inverse first order; their higher-order result allows a rate nearly inverse α order under stronger smoothness conditions. The paper contrasts these rates with the inverse one-third rate in the number of likelihood evaluations for standard nested Monte Carlo estimation of expected information gain. In the numerical studies, the linear deconvolution example used dimension 20 and 30 realizations; the nonlinear elliptic partial differential equation example used 100 prior coordinates, three measurements, and an entropy-evaluation rule with 1,048,576 points. The reported plots show the expected ordering of convergence for Monte Carlo, first-order quasi-Monte Carlo, and tent-transformed second-order quasi-Monte Carlo, but do not give exact numerical error values in the text.

key_equations.explanation: U is the design utility, ξ is the design, Ent is differential entropy, π(·;ξ) is the evidence density, π(·|X;ξ) is the conditional data density, X is the unknown, and E_μ is expectation under prior μ.

key_equations.explanation: π_M^K is the evidence approximation, y is data, ξ is the design, M is the number of mixture components, m indexes those components, 𝒩 is a Gaussian density, G_K is the approximate forward map, x_m is a prior point, and Γ is the noise covariance.

key_equations.name: Entropy estimator
key_equations.explanation: J-hat is the entropy estimate, N is the number of data draws, n indexes the draws, π_M^K is the evidence approximation, Y_n is drawn from that approximation, and ξ is the design.

key_equations.name: Convergence rates
key_equations.explanation: RMSE_MC and RMSE_QMC are the root-mean-squared errors for the Monte Carlo and quasi-Monte Carlo methods; δ_K is forward-model approximation error; M is the number of points building the mixture; N is the number of entropy-estimation draws; and γ is an arbitrarily small positive loss in the quasi-Monte Carlo rate.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors’ theoretical rates rely on conditions such as Gaussian additive noise and regularity or tail assumptions on the prior and forward map. They note that the quasi-Monte Carlo error constants can depend on the input dimension, and that their reported complexity estimates count forward solves rather than the full cost of entropy estimation. Their numerical tests focus on convergence in M and do not systematically test convergence in N or K.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence is limited to two simulated examples, and the nonlinear example compares against a reference computed with a larger numerical run rather than a known exact entropy. The method estimates the utility for a given design, but the paper does not demonstrate the full practical workflow of searching or optimizing over designs when forward solves are expensive. Its usefulness in settings with model misspecification, constrained measurements, or noise whose entropy cannot be calculated is not validated by these experiments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors state that the additional computational overhead associated with their approach will be analyzed in future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to integrate the entropy estimator with an end-to-end design optimization procedure and test how estimation error affects the selected design. Further validation could include real experiments, practical measurement and resource constraints, and noise models beyond the Gaussian examples, along with comparisons of total computation time rather than forward-solve counts alone.

narrate.summary: The paper develops experimental designs for choosing treatment policies when people may affect others in unknown ways within large clusters. Its objective is to estimate how a small change in treatment probabilities affects average outcomes, and then use that information to improve policy choices. The single-wave design pairs comparable clusters and assigns each cluster a slightly higher or lower treatment probability, estimating the policy effect from the paired outcome contrast. The authors also propose a sequential design that updates policies using information from a different cluster pair. In a Pakistan weather-information experiment, effects were substantial around a fifty percent treatment rate but close to zero around seventy percent.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical results give regret that decreases at a rate of one over the number of clusters, up to logarithmic factors, when cluster count grows with the number of iterations; under stronger conditions and much larger per-cluster samples, the paper also establishes exponential out-of-sample improvement. The field experiment covered 25 tehsils and 287,487 farmers, with treatment probabilities perturbed by 10 percentage points around 50% and 70%. For incorrect weather-belief outcomes, the estimated marginal effect was -4.00 at 50% treatment, with a one-sided randomization-test p-value of 0.02; at 70% it was -0.31, with a p-value of 0.41. The authors estimate that treating 70% rather than 100% of farmers could save approximately USD 1 million per year at national scale; a grid design using 0%, 50%, and 100% would instead recommend treating everyone. In calibrated numerical studies with 200 replications, the proposed method produced out-of-sample welfare improvements over the best reported competitor in both applications studied.

key_equations.name: Marginal policy effect and local-perturbation construction
key_equations.explanation: The policy parameter beta indexes treatment probabilities, eta is the perturbation size, W is average outcome under a policy, and M is the marginal policy effect estimated by the central finite difference.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method relies on comparable clusters, limited dependence within clusters, and negligible spillovers across clusters. The authors also note that comparisons across experimental waves require no carryover effects, and that strong within-cluster dependence or unobserved cluster-level differences can prevent learning optimal policies without network information or many independent clusters.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The field evidence comes from 25 tehsils, and the main outcome survey includes 259 observations in the first wave and 583 in the second, so estimates may be imprecise and may not generalize broadly. Forecast-belief accuracy is used as the policy objective, but the experiment does not establish the resulting effects on farm profits or yields.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying settings with spillovers between clusters, methods for estimating clusters from data, and matching clusters on observed characteristics. They also identify analysis of interference that grows with sample size, partially observed networks, and the costs and benefits of collecting network data as future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A practical next step would be to develop and validate implementation software that supports cluster matching, randomization, and the sequential updates used in the design. Further field studies could test the method with explicit budget or capacity constraints and measure downstream outcomes such as farm profits, not only forecast beliefs.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for designing adaptive experiments when the experimenter and regulator may have different objectives, with clinical trials as its main example. The regulator sets a minimum expected social-welfare requirement, and the experimenter chooses the sampling and stopping rules that maximize the experimenter's own payoff while meeting that requirement. The analysis considers two treatments with unknown means, Gaussian priors, and information arriving incrementally through Gaussian signals. Under the paper's main assumptions, the optimal sampling allocation is the Neyman allocation, while the stopping thresholds can be asymmetric when the experimenter receives a fixed benefit from approval. In a clinical-trial calibration, the proposed adaptive design reaches the welfare of a conventional fixed-size trial with substantially fewer observations.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical result is that the Neyman allocation is optimal for all considered objective functions under the stated prior and variance conditions. In the baseline clinical-trial calibration, simulations show that the adaptive design attains the welfare of a conventional randomized controlled trial while using about 48% fewer observations on average; the expected stopping time is about 0.52 in the paper's normalized units. With the paper's assumed median trial size of 300 participants and cost of USD 41,000 per participant, this reduction corresponds to nearly USD 6 million in expected savings, and about 86% of simulated trials stop before the normalized time corresponding to 300 participants. If the regulator instead raises the welfare requirement until the adaptive design has the same average sample size as the conventional trial, the reported welfare gain is 3.2%.

key_equations.name: Incremental Gaussian signal model
key_equations.explanation: For treatment a, z_a is the cumulative signal, gamma is the sampling amount, mu_a is the unknown treatment mean, sigma_a is its known standard deviation, and W_a is standard Brownian motion.

key_equations.name: Experimenter's welfare maximization subject to the regulator's requirement
key_equations.explanation: The experimenter chooses design d to maximize expected utility u_B net of sampling cost c times stopping time tau, subject to expected regulator utility u_A being at least V_0, where delta_d^* is the regulator's optimal decision and mu_1 minus mu_0 is the treatment-effect difference.

key_equations.name: Optimal sampling allocation
key_equations.explanation: The optimal cumulative sampling q_a^* for arm a by time t is its standard deviation sigma_a divided by the sum of the two arms' standard deviations, multiplied by t.

key_equations.name: Optimal stopping rule
key_equations.explanation: The optimal stopping time tau^* is the first time t at which the posterior mean m_t leaves the continuation interval between the lower boundary b^-(t) and upper boundary b^+(t).

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify the common-prior assumption and the linear utility specification as important limitations. The latter implies risk neutrality with respect to treatment-effect magnitude; the authors note that nonlinear returns to treatment effect could strengthen the experimenter's approval bias. Their finite-sample optimality results are asymptotic and rely on model conditions, including a Gaussian prior and known variance quantities in the main analysis.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The main numerical efficiency claim is based on simulated trials calibrated from published estimates and a Gaussian prior, rather than evaluation on trial-level outcome data, so its practical performance under misspecified or heterogeneous treatment-effect distributions is unknown. The central comparison is to a conventional randomized controlled trial at a matched welfare level; the paper does not establish how the method compares with a broad set of current adaptive-trial procedures or with practical constraints such as recruitment limits, safety monitoring, and operational batch schedules.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors say that practical procedures ideally should adapt to, or be invariant to, unknown outcome variances, which their local asymptotic framework does not capture. They discuss a possible forced-exploration stage, such as equal allocation for an initial group of participants, to estimate the variances before applying the proposed design.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the stopping policy with non-Gaussian and misspecified priors, and to compare it prospectively or by replay on real clinical-trial data against established adaptive designs. Further work could also incorporate practical requirements such as safety-based stopping, recruitment and treatment-allocation constraints, and pre-specified operational batches, while providing validated software for implementation.

narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for estimating how treatment effects change with time since intervention in stepped-wedge cluster randomized trials when delayed outcomes are administratively censored. It focuses on settings where a short-term surrogate is recorded for everyone and censoring is independent of the delayed outcome once the surrogate, exposure time, covariates, and calendar period are taken into account. The authors define effects for each exposure time and construct a cross-fitted estimator that combines an outcome regression with an observation model, using the surrogate to recover information lost to censoring. They also derive an efficiency-based criterion for allocating clusters to rollout waves and a history-based adjustment that uses information collected before crossover. Simulations show that the estimator can be precise and well calibrated, while heavily censored later exposure times remain especially difficult to estimate.
narrate.key_results: In the main simulation with 30 clusters, the estimator with the pre-crossover history adjustment had standard deviations of 0.038, 0.059, and 0.126 for the first, third, and fifth exposure-time effects; the reported efficiency-bound standard deviations were 0.039, 0.057, and 0.117. Its standard deviations were within 7% of those from a correctly specified exposure-time mixed model for the first three of five exposure times, while the mixed model’s standard deviation was about 50% lower for the longest exposure time. When effects changed with calendar time and censoring depended strongly on the surrogate, the estimator’s coverage was 0.94 to 0.96, compared with 0.86 to 0.88 for the mixed model. In the trial-calibrated simulation, an allocation of 7, 2, 2, and 12 clusters to the four waves reduced the simulated variance to 0.45 of the trial allocation’s variance for the longest exposure-time effect and to 0.56 for the exposure-averaged effect; the paper also provides an R package and scripts to reproduce its analyses.

key_equations.name: Censoring assumption
key_equations.explanation: The probability P that the delayed outcome is observed, Delta, is assumed not to depend on delayed outcome Y after conditioning on surrogate S, exposure time x, covariates W, and calendar period t.

key_equations.name: Exposure-time effect
key_equations.explanation: The effect Psi at exposure time x is the population average E of the difference between potential delayed outcomes Y(x) and Y(0), among records in the supported calendar periods T_x.

key_equations.name: Surrogate-assisted corrected outcome
key_equations.explanation: The corrected outcome tilde Y adds to outcome regression m a residual correction using observation indicator Delta and observation probability pi, conditional on surrogate S, exposure time x, covariates W, and calendar period t.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the missing-at-random assumption given the surrogate cannot be tested from observed data. If the delayed outcome is never observed in an exposure-by-period overlap cell, the required positivity condition fails and transporting the surrogate bridge from earlier periods requires an additional substantive assumption. Their stated efficiency and allocation results rely on a simplified planning model that ignores heteroscedasticity and within-period variation in observation probabilities.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is based on simulations, including a synthetic replication of the expedited partner therapy trial, rather than evaluation using that trial’s actual individual-level surrogate and delayed-outcome data. The proposed allocation can be very uneven, with as few as two clusters in some waves in the examples, so its practical performance and inference under such sparse waves merit further validation. The estimator also depends on adequate fitted outcome and observation models and sufficient observed outcomes in the late overlap periods, where the paper shows precision can deteriorate substantially.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors leave time-to-event outcomes with continuous administrative censoring, small-sample methods such as wild cluster bootstrap intervals for skewed outcomes, and allocations that perform well across a range of plausible planning inputs for future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the method on real stepped-wedge trials with individual-level surrogate and delayed-outcome data, including checks of sensitivity to departures from the censoring assumption. Further work could assess allocation choices that preserve a minimum practical number of clusters per wave while balancing several exposure-time effects, and validate small-sample inference when late exposure times are represented by very few clusters.

narrate.summary: This tutorial explains how Monte Carlo simulation can help experimenters understand and check control-versus-treatment (A/B) tests and randomized controlled trials. It covers false positives, statistical power, ways to reduce variance, the risks of repeatedly checking results, and comparisons between frequentist and Bayesian analyses. It also describes simulations of treatment spillovers and other effects in social networks, where users' outcomes can influence one another. The examples use simulated data and include Python code, with the accompanying notebook available in a public repository. The paper's main contribution is demonstrating simulations as a practical aid to understanding experimental results, rather than proposing a new optimal experimental design.
narrate.key_results: In 10,000 simulated tests with a 10% base conversion rate, 1,000,000 users per version, and a 0.05 significance level, the reported false positive rate was 0.051. With a 1% relative improvement in the treatment version, estimated power was 0.762 for a one-sided test and about 65% for a two-sided test. When results were checked at three interim analyses using the unadjusted 0.05 threshold, the false positive rate was reported to rise to about 11%; the paper gives a per-analysis threshold of 0.0221 for three equally spaced analyses under Pocock's boundary, and about 5.05% overall for the described Haybittle–Peto approach. The tutorial also illustrates that increasing sample size, using an even allocation when group variances are equal, and adjusting for useful pre-experiment covariates can reduce variance; it does not report a single numerical efficiency comparison for these techniques.

key_equations.name: Bayesian conversion-rate model
key_equations.explanation: theta_A and theta_B are the conversion probabilities for versions A and B, C_A and C_B are their observed conversion counts, N is the number of observations per version, Beta denotes the beta distribution under the paper's flat prior, and p_b is the posterior probability that B's conversion probability is higher.

key_equations.name: Monte Carlo estimate of the Bayesian comparison
key_equations.explanation: The estimated posterior probability p_b is the fraction of M paired draws for which theta_B,m, a draw for B's conversion probability, exceeds theta_A,m, a draw for A's conversion probability; I is one when the condition is true and zero otherwise.

key_equations.name: Simulated false positive rate
key_equations.explanation: The estimated false positive rate is the proportion of S simulated tests whose p-value p_s is below the significance threshold alpha, and I is one when that condition is true and zero otherwise.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the approximate correspondence between frequentist p-values and Bayesian posterior probabilities is not exact, particularly with small samples or strong prior beliefs. They note that heavy-tailed outcome measures may require larger samples, and that trimming, winsorizing, or using medians can change the quantity being estimated and should be chosen before the experiment. They also explain that ordinary tests relying on independence can misrepresent treatment effects in social networks.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical examples are illustrative and depend on particular simulated settings, such as the conversion rate, effect size, sample size, and analysis schedule; the paper does not establish how well those numerical findings transfer to other operating conditions. The network discussion describes mechanisms and a sample graph but does not provide quantitative comparisons of alternative network randomization designs or estimators in this paper.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could systematically compare simulation-based design recommendations across a wider range of outcome distributions, allocation constraints, and treatment effects, including settings with heavy-tailed measures. They could also test the tutorial's recommendations against real experiments and provide reusable software for planning, monitoring, and analyzing experiments with interim checks or network spillovers.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how evaluation rules affect what product teams choose to test in decentralized online experimentation. It models a product team that selects the number of tests and the ambition of ideas, while an experience owner sets the scoring rule and launch threshold. The model compares raw evaluation of test estimates with posterior-mean evaluation, which shrinks noisy estimates toward the average impact. The authors also examine operational data from an Amazon experience before and after it adopted posterior-mean-based evaluation and changed launch criteria in 2024. After the change, testing patterns shifted toward fewer, more precise tests of ideas with more varied true impacts, consistent with the model's predictions.
narrate.key_results: In the theoretical model, raw scoring rewards favorable sampling noise and gives the product team an incentive to run more low-precision tests; posterior-mean scoring removes this reward and encourages a local shift toward fewer, more precise tests of more ambitious ideas. In the Amazon data, the number of tests fell by approximately 15 percent and sampling standard errors fell by over 30 percent for both studied metrics. Estimated dispersion of true impacts roughly doubled for one metric and increased by around 60 percent for the other, producing a more than two-fold increase in the signal-to-noise ratio for both; the estimate for the second metric was statistically significant. The authors estimate that the value of testing increased by approximately 60 percent for both metrics despite more than 50 percent fewer launches. On a different experience that retained raw scoring, test volume increased while precision and impact dispersion remained largely unchanged.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces usage-aware experimental design for settings where an external decision maker, or a fixed decision rule, will act on collected data. Unlike standard Bayesian experimental design, the method evaluates a design by the experimenter’s expected loss under the rule that will actually be used. It accommodates known, uncertain, non-Bayesian, and black-box rules, and learns adaptive designs from simulated experiments. The authors show theoretically that more informative data can increase expected loss when a rule does not use information in a way that aligns with the experimenter’s objective. Simulations in clinical trials, manufacturing inspection, image acquisition, and candidate selection show that designs accounting for the downstream rule can improve outcomes and collect data differently.
narrate.key_results: In the clinical trial example, the learned adaptive design achieved expected utility of 57.79 million euros under the Bonferroni test, compared with 52.27 million euros for the best single-stage design, and reached 99.7% of the dynamic-programming solution; training and first-stage selection took under four minutes, compared with 54 minutes for dynamic programming. In manufacturing inspection, mean loss was 0.265 for the usage-aware policy, versus 0.414 for the best baseline and 0.524 for random inspection. For frozen image classifiers, the usage-aware acquisition policy had the highest test accuracy at every reported precision budget, with the largest advantage when precision was scarce; the paper does not give exact accuracy values in the text. In candidate selection, accounting for a cautious decision rule reduced incompatibility cost by two thirds relative to the knowledge-gradient baseline at the reported caution setting, and policies serving two decision makers improved on specialist-policy comparisons.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the approach in real clinical, manufacturing, or inspection studies, including cases where the assumed likelihood and downstream rule may be misspecified. narrate.summary: The paper proposes a way to train a reasoning large language model to choose informative questions in sequential Bayesian experimental design. Its method, Amortized Reasoning for Bayesian Experimental Design, trains the model’s reasoning and question selection using information-gain rewards evaluated under a fixed generative model that is separate from the acting model. The authors test the approach mainly in Twenty Questions, using a finite set of possible targets and a separate language model to estimate answer likelihoods. They also examine multi-step rewards and transfer to clinical question asking. The method generally improves information acquisition over the reported baselines and shows gains on a simulated clinical dialogue benchmark.
narrate.key_results: For the main Twenty Questions experiments, training used 1,200 partial game histories, a fixed contrastive set of 200 animals, and trajectories built from 100 target animals. Expected-reward training raised animal information gain from 0.290 to 0.330 nats per question and solve rate from 34.0% to 43.3% compared with realized-reward training; it also improved both measures on Plants and Countries, but not Celebrities. In reported timing comparisons, the proposed method took 38.9 seconds per game versus 2,376 seconds for inference-time BED-LLM, and 47.3 seconds per training step versus 136.3 seconds for ASIG. On MediQ, the medically fine-tuned policy’s accuracy rose from 90.5% to 94.7% on held-out dermatology diagnoses and from 84.8% to 90.2% on cases from other specialties; the paper also reports higher correct-answer likelihood and lower Brier scores in both groups.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors study relatively short rollout horizons and identify extending them while maintaining a reliable training signal as an important challenge. They also report sensitivity to the coverage of a misspecified contrastive hypothesis set and call for further study of its size, composition, and prior weighting.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The information rewards depend on a separate language model’s likelihood judgments, so errors or biases in those judgments can train the policy toward misleading questions. The finite hypothesis sets and the use of the oracle’s most likely answer during practical rollouts limit how closely training represents uncertain, open-ended interactions. The clinical evaluation uses simulated patients and a separate decider, and the reported medical policy was trained on synthetic medical question-asking data rather than being the animal-trained policy, so this is not a direct real-world test of cross-task transfer.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the rollout horizon while preserving a reliable training signal. They also identify further investigation of contrastive-set size, composition, and prior weighting as future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the likelihood evaluator against observed response frequencies and test whether the learned questions remain useful when answers are noisy or unavailable. Prospective clinical studies and evaluations with realistic question costs, time limits, and other operational constraints could test practical value beyond the simulated benchmark. It would also be useful to assess sequential adaptation and broader hypothesis spaces with nonuniform prior beliefs.

narrate.summary: This paper studies whether mixed orthogonal arrays with six factors and strength two exist for specified factor levels and run sizes. The authors develop constructions using incomplete orthogonal Latin squares, incomplete transversal designs, and resolvable transversal designs. The work is a theoretical contribution and does not report a data application or software.
narrate.key_results: For six factors at strength two, the run size must be divisible by the least common multiple of the products of every pair of factor levels. For types outside the stated exceptional families, the authors prove that this necessary condition is also sufficient. For one exceptional family, an array exists when the run size is a larger multiple than the necessary minimum; for another family, the paper establishes existence for larger multiples but leaves the minimum-multiple question unresolved in nine cases. The results are theoretical existence statements, not comparisons of prediction accuracy, efficiency, or empirical performance.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes adaptive conditional residual sampling (ACRS) for minimizing expected cost plus a weighted conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) when uncertainty changes with the decision and can be sampled only through a simulator with a fixed draw budget. ACRS takes one simulator draw at each point in a space-filling design, fits a location and scale model, and reuses standardized residuals to create scenarios for a deterministic surrogate objective. It searches the surrogate for promising candidate decisions, adds samples near leading candidates, reranks candidates using shared simulator inputs, and applies local refinement with tail importance sampling. The paper derives a bound on the surrogate minimizer’s optimality gap in terms of the error in its scenario distribution, and establishes consistency results for the refinement estimator. In the reported tests, ACRS generally achieved lower regret than the comparison methods, though its results on held-out problems were comparable to pure local refinement and refinement alone did better on two held-out problems at the smallest budget.
narrate.key_results: On 60 new analytic instances, ACRS had mean normalized regret of 11.8%, compared with 22.3% for cross-entropy search, 22.9% for refinement-only, 26.1% for kernel-density conditional optimization, 29.4% for Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization, and 42.3% for stochastic-gradient optimization. ACRS had mean regret of 10.4% on the three development problems and 0.4% on the two six-dimensional benchmarks; on the three held-out problems its mean regret was 13.5%, equal to refinement-only to one decimal place. Its advantage was largest at the smallest analytic-family budget: mean regret was 24.5% at 2,000 draws, versus at least 40.6% for the comparison methods. Across methods and benchmark families, the median share of the draw budget used was between 96.5% and 99.9%; ACRS typically spent 15–20% on its global phase. The theory bounds surrogate optimality error by a constant times the uniform Wasserstein error of the scenario distribution and establishes consistency of the importance-sampling estimator and convergence of the sample-path objective under stated assumptions.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The initial space-filling design takes only one draw at each decision, so it provides little direct information about local simulation variability or the reliability of the fitted conditional distribution at particular decisions. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose adapting budget allocation between the global and local phases, developing residual models that allow decision-dependent distribution shape, and extending the method to higher-dimensional and constrained problems.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to add diagnostics that assess conditional tail-model fit and identify when the surrogate is unreliable, including comparisons of single-draw designs with replicated designs. narrate.summary: This paper introduces generalised Bayesian optimal experimental design (GBOED), a sequential design method intended to make both design selection and parameter inference more robust to model misspecification. It replaces likelihood-based updating with generalised Bayesian inference (GBI), which uses a loss function to update beliefs. The authors derive the Gibbs expected information gain (GEIG) as the design criterion and give an importance-sampling approach for estimating it. They also propose an exponential decay schedule for a weighting parameter in weighted score matching, so early observations can inform the model before stronger downweighting is applied. In simulations, GBOED often improves predictive performance under outliers and incorrect noise assumptions, while performance depends on the loss function and learning rate.
narrate.key_results: The simulations cover linear regression, pharmacokinetics, constant elasticity of substitution, and location finding, with experiment budgets of 10, 5, 10, and 30, respectively. In linear regression with asymmetric outliers, the exponential-decay GBOED method achieved an MMD of 0.4803, compared with 0.5479 for BOED; in the well-specified case the corresponding values were 0.0768 and 0.1340. For two-dimensional location finding with asymmetric outliers, the exponential-decay method achieved an MMD of 0.0388, compared with 0.1243 for BOED, while BOED was marginally better in the well-specified case, with 0.0001 versus 0.0011. The reported average deployment time for location finding was 49,611.9172 seconds for exponential-decay GBOED and 42,711.3084 seconds for BOED; the authors also report that GBOED can fall behind BOED in well-specified settings, as in pharmacokinetics.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses four simulated design problems and focuses on outliers and error-distribution misspecification, so it does not establish how the approach performs in real experiments or under other forms of model error. Results also depend on problem-specific choices of loss, learning rate, and weighting parameters, making a broadly reliable default difficult to identify from the reported comparisons.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify experimental-design-specific learning-rate selection as a need. They also point to amortising design policies through offline training as a way to support faster online deployment.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method in real industrial experiments and under structural model errors, rather than only the simulated contamination and noise scenarios considered here. They could also develop procedures that adapt the loss and its tuning parameters as data arrive, and evaluate the method when practical design constraints limit the available experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a design for multi-arm randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that aims to identify local average treatment effects (LATEs) when subjects may not receive their assigned treatments. It first shows that, with three or more arms, conventional randomization cannot identify nontrivial effects comparing the same two treatments for a common group under several strong compliance restrictions. The proposed design asks subjects to report their favorite arm and then randomizes assignment conditional on that report. If subjects receive only the assigned arm or their reported favorite, comparing assignment groups within a report group restores a one-sided compliance structure. The paper derives a Wald-type formula for the effect of the reported favorite versus an alternative among subjects in that report group who accept the alternative.
narrate.key_results: For three or more arms, the paper proves that conventional randomization does not identify nontrivial margin-specific group effects, even when ordered monotonicity, strict stability, and unordered monotonicity all hold. Under the proposed design, the reported favorite can be truthfully elicited by tilting assignment probabilities toward the report, and the identified effect is for reported-favorite subjects who comply with assignment to the alternative arm. The paper reports theoretical identification results rather than numerical estimates, efficiency comparisons, or run-size comparisons. It also gives a choice model in which positive costs of deviating from assignment generate transitive compliance, a broad class of behavior that motivates the design.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future research could evaluate the protocol in field experiments and measure how often the reported-favorite compliance restriction is credible in different administrative settings. It could also develop sensitivity analyses and finite-sample inference procedures for deviations from that restriction, including cases where treatment switching cannot be fully controlled.

glossary.meaning: Bayesian experimental design: choosing experiments to maximize expected value of the resulting data.
The paper’s fairness-aware Bayesian experimental design framework.
Expected information gain: the expected reduction in uncertainty about a target.
Expected predictive information gain: expected information about predictions at future test inputs.
Theta is the target quantity; phi is the sensitive attribute.
D is the acquired dataset, omega is the context used to assess fairness, and pi is the data acquisition policy.
The coefficient controlling how strongly the objective penalizes a fairness-related information measure.
F denotes a fairness penalty, R denotes the combined design objective, and I denotes the selected fairness penalty.

narrate.summary: FairBED extends Bayesian experimental design by choosing data that are useful for learning a target while limiting information that could support unfair predictions about a sensitive attribute. It defines fairness relative to a hypothetical fair world in which the target and sensitive attribute are initially unrelated, given the relevant context. The method penalizes either the relationship between those quantities learned from the data, information the data reveal about the sensitive attribute, or both, while rewarding information about the target. The authors adapt the approach to sequential data acquisition and active learning, where the system selects which cases to label. Simulations and benchmark datasets show that the method can improve measured fairness and accuracy trade-offs over random sampling and conventional information-seeking design.
narrate.key_results: In the source-location simulation with 10 experiments, the conditional fairness objective reduced coupling by 96% relative to standard Bayesian experimental design at the strongest reported penalty setting for adaptive policies. In active learning, using up to 200 labels on the synthetic task and 400 on each of two benchmark datasets, the coupling-focused objective reduced attribute sensitivity by up to 17%, 26%, and 33% at the same target accuracy on the synthetic, census, and student-graduation tasks. The sensitive-attribute information objective reduced an adversary’s sensitive-attribute test accuracy by up to 5.5 percentage points on the census data and 1.8 points on the synthetic data. On the synthetic task, the reduction in attribute sensitivity also transferred to different downstream model classes, falling by 43% to 57% from the expected predictive information gain baseline to the strongest reported penalty setting.

key_equations.name: Fair-world model
key_equations.explanation: The joint model factors into the probability of context omega, the conditional probabilities of target theta and sensitive attribute phi given omega, and the probability of dataset D given theta, phi, omega, and acquisition policy pi.

key_equations.name: Expected coupling penalty
key_equations.explanation: F with subscripts theta and phi is the expected coupling penalty, the expectation over context omega and data D generated under policy pi of the conditional mutual information I between target theta and sensitive attribute phi given D and omega.

key_equations.name: FairBED design objective
key_equations.explanation: R with subscript I is the objective for policy pi, equal to expected information gain about target theta minus beta times the chosen fairness penalty I.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their fairness formalization is one possible approach, not the only way to measure fairness. They note that context selection affects which dependencies are treated as acceptable, and that fairness penalties can reduce accuracy, data diversity, or representation of some groups. They also caution that adaptively acquired data are not a random sample, so naive frequentist estimates of population quantities can be biased.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation covers one simulated design problem and three active-learning tasks, so it does not establish how the method performs in prospective industrial or clinical experiments. Its active-learning results depend on an assessment model capable of representing dependence between the outcome and sensitive label; real applications may have too few labels or unreliable sensitive-attribute measurements to estimate that dependence well. Reported fairness measures are model-based proxies and do not directly establish reductions in downstream harm.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Test the method in prospective experiments and broader domains, including cases where sensitive labels are incomplete or costly to collect. Evaluate explicit constraints on group representation, per-group prediction quality, and acquisition cost alongside the information-based penalties. Compare the approach with additional fairness criteria and examine robustness when the assessment model or deployment population differs from the one used during design.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how to rank a finite set of treatment saturations, where a saturation is the share of units treated in each cluster. It considers a two-stage randomized saturation experiment and evaluates the empirical success ranking, which orders saturations by their estimated mean welfare. The design and analysis allow arbitrary interference among units within a cluster, while requiring no network data and excluding interference between clusters. The authors derive finite-sample regret bounds and a local asymptotic comparison with the best possible ranking rule, then use the bounds to propose how to allocate clusters across saturation arms. They find that ranking efficient welfare estimates is within a factor of 1.42 of the local minimax benchmark, and the Malawi application shows that the realized allocation was close to the allocation minimizing their bound.
narrate.key_results: The finite-sample bound limits the probability of reversing a pair of saturations by an exponential function of their welfare gap and the number of clusters in each arm; with 922 clusters per arm, a pair separated by a welfare gap of 0.05 is ordered correctly with probability at least 0.9 under the stated bound. In the local asymptotic analysis, the maximum regret of the ranking based on efficient welfare estimates is at most 1.42 times the minimax regret for any number of saturations and any covariance; with two saturations it is exactly minimax. In simulations with four saturations, scaled regret was close to the Gaussian benchmark from eight clusters onward, while the finite-sample bounds were conservative. In the Malawi application, the plug-in regret bound for the realized design was 0.06 to 0.07, and reallocation reduced it by only 2.3% to 3.6%; the authors report that halving the bound would require four times as many programme areas, or 352 rather than 88.

key_equations.name: Reduced cluster-mean model
key_equations.explanation: X is the observed cluster mean in saturation arm k and cluster position r, U is the welfare of arm k, and E denotes expectation; the observations are independent across arm positions and bounded between zero and one.

key_equations.name: Finite-sample pairwise regret bound
key_equations.explanation: R_ES is expected ranking regret, the sum is over every pair of distinct saturation arms k and k-prime, Δ is their absolute welfare gap, C_k and C_k-prime are their cluster counts, and exp is the exponential function.

key_equations.name: Cluster-allocation objective
key_equations.explanation: G is the allocation objective, summed over pairs of saturation arms; m is the vector of arm cluster counts, v is the vector of cluster-mean variances, and the square-root terms are the standard deviations of estimated welfare contrasts.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors assume partial interference, so outcomes may depend on treatment within a cluster but not on treatment in other clusters. They do not characterize the exact minimax regret for three or more saturations, and state that allocating clusters under the efficient covariance would require a separate derivation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The proposed allocation is derived for a reduced experiment and depends on variance and cost inputs; actual experiments may also have blocking, minimum arm sizes, integer constraints, or other design restrictions that need to be incorporated. The numerical comparisons cover a four-saturation simulation setup and one application, so they provide limited evidence about performance across different menus, outcome distributions, and operational settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying spillovers between clusters, adaptive or multi-wave designs that allocate later clusters to comparisons that remain unresolved, and saturation rules that depend on cluster covariates. They also identify the exact minimax ranking rule and allocation under the efficient covariance as open questions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could develop allocation procedures that directly handle blocking, integer arm sizes, minimum cluster counts, and uncertain variance estimates, then test them in prospective randomized experiments. It would also be useful to assess robustness when outcomes are unbounded or when the assumed within-cluster assignment rule differs from implementation.
